In recent years, it has been shown that various DRO formulations of learning models admit tractable convex reformulations. However, most existing works propose to solve these convex reformulations by general-purpose solvers, which are problems and propose two novel epigraphical projection-based incremental algorithms to solve them. The updates in each iteration of these algorithms can be determined growth exponents. Consequently, we are able to establish the convergence rates of the proposed incremental algorithms. Many popular GNNs fail to generalize to this setting, and are even outperformed by models that ignore the graph structure (e.g., multilayer perceptrons). Motivated by this limitation, we identify a set of key designs—ego- and heterophily. We combine them into a graph neural network, H2 GCN, which we designs. institution_raw: Department of Computer Science Columbia University New York, NY Learning causal effects from data is a fundamental problem across the sciences. Determining the identifiability of a target effect from a combination of the observational distribution and the causal graph underlying a phenomenon is wellunderstood in theory. However, in practice, it remains a challenge to apply the identification theory to estimate the identified causal functionals from finite samples. Although a plethora of effective estimators have been developed under the still no systematic way of estimating arbitrary causal functionals that are both computationally and statistically attractive. This paper aims to bridge this gap, from causal identification to causal estimation. We note that estimating functionals from limited samples based on the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle from the generality of the causal identification theory and the effectiveness of the estimators produced based on the principle of ERM. Specifically, we develop a practical procedure for learning causal effects from finite samples and a causal graph. Finally, experimental results support the effectiveness of our approach. institution_raw: Department of Computer Science Northwestern University Evanston, IL, USA Given a set of n data points in Euclidean space, our goal is to partition them into k clusters (each characterized by a center), such that the sum of squares of distances of data points to their nearest is defined by the initial set of centers, called a seed. Arthur and Vassilvitskii ( ) and Ostrovsky, and then choosing the subsequent k centers by randomly sampling a single point in each round with the sampling probability of every point proportional to its current cost. That is, the probability of choosing any data point x is proportional to the squared distance to its closest already chosen center. Due to its speed, simplicity, and good empirical performance, k-means++ is the most widely used Spark MLlib, Google BigQuery, IBM SPSS, Intel DAAL, and Microsoft ML.NET. In addition to k-means++, these libraries implement a scalable variant of k-means++ called k-meansk (read “kmeans parallel”) designed by Bahmani, Moseley, Vattani, Kumar, and Vassilvitskii ( ). Somewhat However, theoretical guarantees for k-meansk are substantially weaker than for k-means++. independently draws approximately ` = ⇥(k) random centers according to the D2 distribution.
